What must you do?","fact_ids":["sec09-F02"]},"answer":{"text":"Stop and confirm no train is coming, unless signs say otherwise.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02"]},"rationale":{"text":"School buses must stop at crossings even without a stop sign or signal.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Reading a railroad crossing","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Some crossings require a stop.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F05"]},{"text":"Some vehicles always stop.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F05"]},{"text":"Passive or active warnings.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about railroad crossings and what each kind asks of you. Some crossings have a stop sign. Some vehicles must stop at every crossing, sign or no sign. And crossings come in two types: passive crossings, which rely on signs and markings, and active crossings, which add gates, lights or bells. Knowing which type you are approaching tells you how much of the checking is up to you. Practice questions often describe a crossing or a vehicle and ask whether a stop is required, so we will connect each situation to its rule as we go.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Stop signs and special vehicles","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop sign: stop, train or not.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02"]},{"text":"Buses and hire vehicles stop.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02"]},{"text":"Hazardous-material haulers stop.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"A stop sign at a railroad crossing means you must stop, even when no train is visible. Unless signs say otherwise, school buses, for-hire passenger vehicles, gasoline trucks and other vehicles hauling hazardous materials must stop and confirm no train is coming, even without a stop sign or signal. These vehicles carry passengers or dangerous loads, so a crash would be especially severe. If you drive behind one, expect it to stop at the crossing, and leave room for it to do so.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Passive crossings","fact_ids":["sec09-F03","sec09-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"No lights or gates.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03","sec09-F04"]},{"text":"Signs, markings and crossbucks.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03","sec09-F04"]},{"text":"You yield and check every track.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03","sec09-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Passive crossings have no flashing lights or gates. They rely on advance warning signs, pavement markings, and crossbucks with yield or stop signs at or just before the tracks. Because nothing will warn you that a train is coming, you must do the checking. At a passive crossing, slow or stop as needed, yield to trains, check both directions, make sure every track is clear, and never race a train. Where there are several tracks, a train on one can hide a second train on another, which is why every track must be clear before you go.","fact_ids":["sec09-F03","sec09-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Active crossings","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Gates, flashing lights.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]},{"text":"Message signs, bells or sounds.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]},{"text":"They announce a train.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Active crossings warn of a train with some mix of gates, flashing lights, message signs, and bells or other sounds. When these devices activate, they are telling you a train is approaching. The equipment does part of the work that you must do yourself at a passive crossing. But an active crossing does not replace your own attention. You still look both ways as you approach, and you still treat a quiet crossing with care. The next lesson covers exactly what to do when the signals at an active crossing start, and how long to wait after a train passes.","fact_ids":["sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"No gates does not mean safe","fact_ids":["sec09-R07","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Trap: no signals, so no train.","fact_ids":["sec09-R07","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05"]},{"text":"Passive: signs and markings only.","fact_ids":["sec09-R07","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05"]},{"text":"You must look and yield.","fact_ids":["sec09-R07","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Passive crossings use signs and markings only, while active crossings add gates, flashing lights or bells that announce a train. At a passive crossing, the absence of lights and gates says nothing about whether a train is coming. It only means no device will warn you. Options may suggest that a crossing with no signals is rarely used, or that you may cross without slowing. Both are wrong. At a passive crossing, slow or stop as needed, check both directions, make sure every track is clear, and yield to the train. A quiet crossing is not a green light.","fact_ids":["sec09-R07","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check a school bus","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"School bus, crossing ahead.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F01"]},{"text":"No stop sign or signal.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are driving a school bus toward a railroad crossing that has no stop sign and no signal. So the answer is to stop and confirm that no train is coming before you cross. An ordinary car at the same crossing would slow, look and yield, but the bus must come to a stop first.","fact_ids":["sec09-F02","sec09-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Crossing types recap","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop sign means stop.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]},{"text":"Buses and hazmat always stop.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]},{"text":"Signs only versus signals.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"To finish, a stop sign at a railroad crossing means you must stop even when no train is visible. Passive crossings rely on advance warning signs, pavement markings and crossbucks, so you slow or stop, yield, check both directions and every track, and never race a train. Active crossings add gates, flashing lights, message signs and bells. The hook is signs only versus signals.","fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec09-u02","module_id":"sec09-m02","objective_ids":["sec09-u02"],"title":{"text":"Crossing tracks safely","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Activated signals mean a train is about twenty seconds away, so you stop and never go around the gates.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"A second train can follow the first, so you wait until gates rise and every track is clear.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},{"text":"Stopping on tracks can trap you, so you cross only when your vehicle can clear the far side.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F10"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Mei approaches a crossing as traffic beyond it backs up toward the tracks.","fact_ids":["sec09-F10"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Do not start across unless your vehicle can clear the far side of the tracks by at least six feet.","fact_ids":["sec09-F10","sec09-R08"]},"result":{"text":"Mei waits before the crossing until there is room for her whole car plus six feet on the far side.","fact_ids":["sec09-F10"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Myth: once the train has passed, you may go even if the gates are still down.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},"correction":{"text":"After a train passes, wait until the gates rise, lights and bells stop, and you are sure all tracks are clear.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Six feet, twenty seconds.","fact_ids":["sec09-R08"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You hear a train horn as you near a crossing. Roughly how much time do you have?","fact_ids":["sec09-F11"]},"answer":{"text":"About twenty seconds before the train arrives.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-R08"]},"rationale":{"text":"Once lights and gates activate or you hear a horn, you have about twenty seconds, which is not enough to risk crossing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F11","sec09-F06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Crossing without risk","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop for activated signals.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"Wait for all clear.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"Never get trapped on tracks.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers how to cross railroad tracks safely. We will look at what to do when crossing signals activate, how long to wait after a train passes, the habits that keep you moving while you are on the tracks, how to handle snow, and the rule for backed-up traffic beyond a crossing. Two numbers anchor the lesson: the six feet of clearance you need on the far side, and the roughly twenty seconds of warning you get when signals start. Practice questions often mix those two numbers up, so we will keep them firmly apart and tie each one to its own rule.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When signals activate","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Bells, lights or a moving gate: stop.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"Never through, around or under.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"About twenty seconds of warning.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Stop whenever crossing bells ring, lights flash, or the gate is down or moving. Once crossing lights and gates activate or you hear a train horn, you have about twenty seconds before the train arrives. That is very little time, and a train is closer and faster than it looks. Driving around a lowered gate to save a minute risks everything for nothing. Treat activated signals as an absolute stop, and stay stopped until the next slide's conditions are met.","fact_ids":["sec09-F06","sec09-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"After the train passes","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Wait for gates to rise.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},{"text":"Wait for lights and bells to stop.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},{"text":"Be sure all tracks are clear.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"After a train passes, wait until the gates rise, the lights and bells stop, and you are sure all tracks are clear. So the end of one train is not the end of the danger. Look both ways again before you move. Only when the gates are up, the signals are quiet and you can see every track clearly is it time to cross. Patience here is what prevents the second-train crash. Two trains can share one crossing.","fact_ids":["sec09-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"On the tracks","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Never stop on tracks.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09"]},{"text":"Expect a train; look both ways.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09"]},{"text":"No gear changes; keep speed in snow.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Never stop on the tracks, always expect a train, look both ways, and avoid changing gears while crossing. Choose your moment, look, and then cross smoothly without stopping, without shifting, and without losing so much speed that the snow can hold you.","fact_ids":["sec09-F08","sec09-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Room on the far side","fact_ids":["sec09-F10","sec09-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Traffic backed up past the crossing?","fact_ids":["sec09-F10","sec09-R08"]},{"text":"Clear the far side by six feet.","fact_ids":["sec09-F10","sec09-R08"]},{"text":"Otherwise wait before the tracks.","fact_ids":["sec09-F10","sec09-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"When traffic may be backed up near a crossing, do not start across unless your vehicle can clear the far side of the tracks by at least six feet. The danger is getting halfway across and then having to stop because the line ahead is not moving. That leaves you on the tracks. So before you start, look past the crossing and make sure there is room for your entire vehicle, plus six feet, beyond the last rail. If there is not, wait before the tracks, behind the stop line, until the line moves forward. Never let the car ahead pull you onto the tracks.","fact_ids":["sec09-F10","sec09-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u02-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Six feet or twenty seconds","fact_ids":["sec09-R08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Trap: swapping the two numbers.","fact_ids":["sec09-R08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"Six feet of clearance.","fact_ids":["sec09-R08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]},{"text":"About twenty seconds of warning.","fact_ids":["sec09-R08","sec09-F10","sec09-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. It is rare, but the right response is simple and must be quick. The first step is always the same: get everyone out and away from the tracks. What you do next depends on whether a train is coming or the signals are active. We will cover both cases, then look at the blue Emergency Notification Sign that sits at or near crossings, what information it gives you, and what railroad officials can do once you call. Questions here usually test the order of steps and which number to call.","fact_ids":["sec09-F12","sec09-F13","sec09-F14","sec09-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec09-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Two cases, one first step","fact_ids":["sec09-F12","sec09-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Train coming or gates active: out, then call nine one one.","fact_ids":["sec09-F12","sec09-F13"]},{"text":"No train, nothing active: out, then the railroad.","fact_ids":["sec09-F12","sec09-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"If you are stuck on the tracks and the gates are activated or a train is clearly coming, get everyone out and far from the tracks right away, then call nine one one. When you call and give that ID, railroad officials know exactly which crossing you mean. They may slow, stop or divert a train. After calling the railroad, you then call nine one one. If no train is in sight and nothing is activated, get everyone out and call the railroad emergency number on the blue sign.
